speaker: Jeff Currie
title: Jeff Currie on the 'Volatility Trap' Keeping Commodity Prices So High
question: In commodity finance, why do post-2008 bank leverage ratios constrain lending right when commodity prices surge?
guest: It really boils down to leverage ratios, which were put in place in Dodd-Frank following 2008 and 2009. Think about what that leverage ratio is: it's Tier 1 capital on the top and the total assets of the bank on the bottom. What is Tier 1 capital? It's bonds. What are all the assets that go into the economy, all that lending? It's based off commodities—things in the real world. Most policymakers will tell you it's inflation-proof because you have the price level times the bonds in the numerator and the price level times overall assets in the denominator, so the price level drops out. The reality is it is not. Why? Because bond prices are negatively impacted by commodity prices. So essentially, that ratio is bonds on the top and commodities on the bottom. What we're seeing is that these leverage ratios start to become really binding. Think about how much more capital the market needs when oil prices are 2X what they were a year ago: you're going to need two times the amount of working capital out there, in an environment where you're already bumping up against those constraints in banking.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The core problem is that the Basel III leverage ratio is risk-insensitive, while commodity financing needs scale mechanically with prices.

Commodity trade finance is largely volume-based: a trader shipping the same cargo of oil or wheat needs a letter of credit, inventory loan or borrowing-base facility sized to the cargo's dollar value. When prices double, the same physical flow requires roughly twice the credit. Higher prices and volatility also trigger large margin calls on hedges, so traders draw on credit lines to fund them, further inflating bank exposures.

The leverage ratio requires Tier 1 capital against total exposure, regardless of risk. Short-dated, self-liquidating, well-collateralised trade loans therefore get no credit for their safety, and off-balance-sheet items such as letters of credit and undrawn commitments are counted too. Bank capital does not rise with commodity prices, so the denominator balloons while the numerator stays fixed.

Because this is a low-margin business, it earns poor returns on leverage-constrained capital, so banks ration it, favouring the largest clients. Internal country, sector and counterparty limits fixed in dollar terms bind at the same moment. The squeeze was seen in 2021–22.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Post-2008 Basel III leverage ratios require banks to hold Tier 1 capital against gross exposures—including loans, letters of credit, and derivatives—without adjusting for risk. Because commodity trade finance is short-term, hedged, and collateralized by physical cargo, it carries low credit risk and earns thin margins, making it difficult to justify balance-sheet usage under a risk-insensitive cap.

When commodity prices surge, this constraint binds from multiple directions at once. Financing the exact same physical volume of cargo suddenly requires proportionally larger nominal loans and letters of credit. Simultaneously, physical traders hedge their inventories using short futures and swaps; spiking prices trigger heavy variation and initial margin calls on those hedges, forcing traders to draw down committed bank credit lines while inflating banks’ own derivative and client-clearing exposure measures. Because bank equity cannot expand overnight, surging nominal credit demand and derivative exposures rapidly exhaust leverage-ratio headroom, prompting banks to ration low-margin commodity lending right when market liquidity is needed most.

noweb.answer: Post-2008 Basel III rules introduced a non-risk-weighted leverage ratio that caps a bank’s total nominal on- and off-balance-sheet exposures relative to Tier 1 capital, regardless of underlying credit risk. Commodity trade finance relies heavily on short-term, self-liquidating, physically collateralized loans, repos, and letters of credit, yet the leverage ratio treats each dollar of these safe, low-margin facilities identically to risky unsecured lending. When commodity prices surge, two mechanical pressures rapidly consume this fixed balance-sheet capacity. First, moving the exact same physical volume of oil, metals, or grain suddenly requires proportionally larger nominal credit lines and trade guarantees. Second, commodity merchants routinely hedge physical inventories with short futures; spiking prices push those hedges deeply out of the money, triggering massive variation and initial margin calls from clearinghouses. As traders draw down revolving credit lines to post cash margin—while higher prices and volatility simultaneously swell banks’ own derivative clearing exposures—nominal balance sheets balloon far faster than bank equity can grow, causing the leverage ratio to bind and forcing banks to ration credit right when liquidity demand peaks.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Commodity trade finance is sized to the value of the goods. Borrowing-base facilities, letters of credit and repo lines grow with the dollar value of the cargo, inventory or receivables they finance. If oil or gas prices double, a trader needs roughly twice as much credit to move the same physical volume. At the same time, volatile prices bring large margin calls on the trader's hedges, and those also have to be funded.

Basel III's leverage ratio, a minimum of 3% plus extra buffers for the biggest banks, limits a bank's total exposure regardless of risk. Short-term, collateralised, self-liquidating trade loans have very low risk weights, but under the leverage ratio they use up as much capital as risky assets. Off-balance-sheet guarantees and derivative exposures also expand when prices and volatility rise. So a price surge inflates the bank's exposure measure without making the business any riskier or more profitable. With a fixed capital base, banks have to ration credit, cut facility limits or charge more, often most sharply at quarter-ends.

The result is procyclical. Credit gets tight exactly when traders need it most, as in 2022, when European energy traders and utilities turned to government and central-bank liquidity support.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Post-2008 Basel III leverage ratios measure a bank’s Tier 1 capital against its total on- and off-balance-sheet exposures without adjusting for risk. Because commodity trade finance is typically short-term, self-liquidating, and backed by physical collateral, it carries relatively low risk weights under traditional capital rules, yet every dollar of lending or letter-of-credit issuance still consumes full balance-sheet capacity under the non-risk-weighted leverage ratio. When commodity prices surge, trading firms need much larger dollar credit lines just to finance the same physical volumes, while rising prices also trigger heavy variation margin calls on their futures hedges that sharply increase demand for bank liquidity. Because banks cannot quickly raise Tier 1 capital to expand their balance sheets, a sudden jump in nominal dollar exposures pushes them against their leverage ceilings. Facing a binding balance-sheet constraint, banks often ration low-margin, high-volume trade finance, pulling back lending precisely when surging prices make credit demand peak.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
When commodity prices surge, traders need more cash to finance the same physical volume. A cargo costs more to buy and carry, and traders who hedge with short futures may have to post cash margin before they receive the proceeds from selling the cargo. Both effects increase demand for bank credit.

The post-2008 Basel III leverage ratio requires banks to hold a minimum amount of Tier 1 capital against their total measured exposure. A larger loan uses more of that capacity even if it is short-term and backed by commodities whose value has also risen. Bank capital typically cannot grow as quickly as traders’ financing needs, so banks close to their leverage limits may cap credit lines or charge more just as traders need to borrow more.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer: A bank’s leverage ratio requires it to hold a minimum amount of capital against its total exposures, regardless of how risky each loan is. When commodity prices surge, financing the same cargo takes a larger loan, and traders may also draw on credit lines to meet margin calls on their hedges. Those draws increase the bank’s exposure while its capital can take time to raise. Even if the cargo fully secures the loan, its value generally does little to reduce the exposure counted for the leverage ratio. A bank near its minimum therefore has to raise capital, shrink other exposures, or limit new lending just as traders need more cash.
